doc.title: Candido Camero — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Learning bongos from his uncle on milk cans
summary: His uncle, a professional in a septet, taught him bongos at four on empty milk cans; his father taught tres and his mother sang. His grandfather predicted he would be famous.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Tell us some of your fond memories of your parents and your childhood.

Well when I was four, my uncle - his name is Andres Guerra Cardenas - was the one who taught me to play the bongos. The way I learned to play the bongos - I was four years old - was with two empty cans of milk. My uncle made me repeat what he played on the bongos. He’d make me repeat what I heard him play and I’d repeat it on the empty condensed milk cans and that was my first inspiration. That gave me inspiration to continue learning aside from the fact that I was in school, too. I was still in Kindergarten. But whenever I came home, I asked my uncle to teach me to play the bongos.
Was your uncle a professional musician?

My mother's brother, he was a professional. And he made a living playing music with a septet called Segundo Nacional. He’d take me to the radio broadcasts and to parties so I could hear how he played. Then I went to school and when I came back from school, I’d repeat what I heard him play at the parties, at the broadcasts, what he taught me at home and so on.
Do you have any memory of the specific groups that you saw play, or you saw at that early age playing with your uncle?

Well yes - Septeto Habanero, Septeto Nacional, Septeto Bologna, Septeto Cauto - were many - the Sonora Matancera - there were many septets. They were all good in that era, very good - different styles.
And so he as a musician, was known to all of the members of these groups, so from a very young age, you were around professional musicians, right?

Yes, from my mom’s side and from my dad’s side. On my mom’s side, my uncles were all musicians. And on my dad’s side, he taught me to play the tres. My uncle taught me to play the bongos and my mom sang. So I imitated all of them. I wanted to be the one-man-band.
Apparently you had a gift and your parents and uncle recognized that talent in you.

Indeed, because when I came home from school - I was still in kindergarten - so, I returned from school at lunch or mealtime. I’d pretend to play bongos on the table. And my mom told me, "It's time to eat, not music time. What are you going to do, eat or play?" And I’d say, "A little of both. I will eat and then I'll play a little." And that’s how I began. So my grandfather told my mother, "Let him be because I know he will be famous someday.” And indeed, I wish he lived long enough for me to have been able to say to him, “Grandfather, you were right."
